name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 25 October 1969

solutions.check: 30 entries, 54 crossings, 0 conflicts, agrees with the 1 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Dreamer inclined to give Rose the hump!

blocks.clueFragment: Dreamer inclined to give Rose the hump!
blocks.note: surface reading: someone with their head in the clouds who keeps annoying a woman called Rose
setter's reading: the classical god of dreams and sleep, whose gift is to send people off and stop them rising

explanation.surface: An idle daydreamer keeps getting on Rose's nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: Rose is the past tense of rise, not a name: the god of sleep keeps a sleeper from getting up, and 'give the hump' is British slang for annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: In Ovid's Metamorphoses this figure is the god who shapes dreams, so he is the dreamer of mythology.

clue.text: Have a bite!

blocks.note: surface reading: an invitation to taste some food
setter's reading: a bite is itself a small mouthful, so the clue simply describes the noun

explanation.definitionFit: A small mouthful of food is exactly the quantity taken in one bite, a tiny portion or scrap.

clue.text: Do away with class distinction at school

blocks.note: first meaning: to take something away or get rid of it
second meaning: in some British schools this is the name of a particular form, an intermediate class

explanation.surface: A reformer wants to abolish class snobbery in schools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class distinction' sounds like social snobbery; in some British public schools a remove is a form or class between two others.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means eliminate or get rid of, and the noun names a school form in certain British schools.

clue.text: Fowl play, the oppressed spouse might consider it

definitions.text: Fowl play, the oppressed spouse might consider it

blocks.note: a pun on 'foul play': what a chicken does with its beak

blocks.clueFragment: the oppressed spouse might consider it
blocks.note: setter's reading: a husband bossed about by his wife feels he is suffering this nagging treatment

explanation.surface: A downtrodden husband regards his treatment as foul play.
explanation.walkthrough: The word splits into a bird and its jab, which is 'fowl play'; as a whole it means to nag a husband constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: A dominating wife who nags and bullies her husband is said to do this to him, the image being a hen jabbing.

clue.text: One to trust with investments

blocks.note: first meaning: a single item, the number one
second meaning: the word placed before 'trust' names a pooled investment fund

explanation.surface: Someone is looking for a person they can trust with their money.
explanation.walkthrough: A unit trust is a British pooled investment fund, so the answer is the word you add to 'trust'.
explanation.definitionFit: A single whole quantity is called this, and it is also the first half of the name of a pooled investment fund.

clue.text: One couldn't do this to a snake in Ireland!

definitions.text: One couldn't do this to a snake in Ireland!

blocks.clueFragment: One couldn't do this to a snake in Ireland!
blocks.note: surface reading: a joke about there being no snakes in Ireland to deal with
setter's reading: Macbeth's line about wounding a serpent without killing it uses the verb wanted, which also names a whisky country

explanation.surface: A joke about Ireland famously having no snakes to deal with.
explanation.walkthrough: Ireland is the misdirection away from Scotland; the verb means to wound or put an end to, as in Macbeth's line.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to wound, crush or put a stop to something, as Macbeth uses it of a snake.

clue.text: Charing can cause annoyance

indicators.note: the preceding word is the raw material that is made into something else, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written; Charing Cross is a London station

explanation.surface: The London district of Charing proves a source of irritation.
explanation.definitionFit: This word names vexation or embarrassed disappointment, a feeling close to irritation.

clue.text: Give temporary relief -when the festival is done

blocks.note: first meaning: help someone through a difficult period for a while
second meaning: tide is an old word for a festival season, as in Yuletide, and over means finished

explanation.surface: Someone offers short-term help once the holidays have ended.
explanation.walkthrough: Tide as a season survives in Yuletide, Eastertide and Whitsuntide.
explanation.definitionFit: To help someone manage through a short difficult spell, such as with a loan, is this phrasal verb.

clue.text: "And is the only dog, my duck" (Hen. V)

definitions.text: "And is the only dog, my duck" (Hen. V)

blocks.clueFragment: "And is the only dog, my duck"
blocks.note: surface reading: an odd line of verse about a dog and a duck
setter's reading: Pistol's proverb in Henry V, 'Brag is a good dog, but ___ is the only dog, my duck', with the missing word wanted

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a quotation with its first word missing; Pistol means that holding on firmly is better than boasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Pistol's proverb names the firm grip, steadfastness, as the best dog of all, punning on a dog's name.

clue.text: Tell-tale?

blocks.note: surface reading: a sneak who reports others' misdeeds
setter's reading: a tale that tells of love and adventure, the kind of story a romance is

explanation.walkthrough: A tell-tale usually means a sneak; here it is read as the sort of story told, a romance.
explanation.definitionFit: A romance is a story of love or adventure, so a story-telling kind of tale is described by the adjective.

clue.text: The old . baggage, as Hamlet might have said

blocks.note: surface reading: an insulting name for an elderly woman
setter's reading: the archaic word for a bundle or burden

explanation.surface: A sneer at an old bag, phrased as Hamlet would put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old baggage' sounds like an insult to a woman; it really means an archaic word for luggage.
explanation.definitionFit: This archaic noun means a bundle or burden, the kind of pack carried on the back.

clue.text: Beaver hats with perforated tops?

definitions.note: describes the nouns: shaker pots with holes in the lid

blocks.note: first meaning: a castor was a hat made of beaver fur, castor being Latin for beaver
second meaning: small pots with holed lids for sprinkling sugar or pepper

explanation.surface: Beaver-fur hats with holes poked through the crowns.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names old beaver-fur hats and also cruet shakers for sprinkling sugar or condiments.

clue.text: Strive in the ultimate to be coveted

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits wholly inside it, so these letters go inside the next word's

blocks.note: to vie is to strive or compete
the ultimate thing is the end

explanation.surface: Striving to the very last for something everyone wants.
explanation.definitionFit: To covet is to long for what belongs to another, so a coveted thing is one people were jealous of.

clue.text: Abduct, with aplomb apparently

definitions.note: describes how the act is done; the phrase means to manage something with aplomb

blocks.note: first meaning: to seize and take someone away
second meaning: to handle a tricky situation successfully, appearing calm and confident

explanation.surface: A kidnapping done coolly and confidently.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to take away by force, and also to succeed at something difficult with apparent confidence.

clue.text: Courageous enough to have picked a flower

blocks.note: first meaning: having pluck, an informal word for nerve or courage
second meaning: pulled off a plant, as a flower is

explanation.surface: Someone brave enough to pick a forbidden flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plucked' as an adjective for brave is mostly British, usually in the phrase 'well plucked'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having pluck means having spirit or nerve, and to pull off a petal or bloom is also this verb.

clue.text: Do they resolve deadlocks?

blocks.note: surface reading: negotiators or mediators who break a stalemate
setter's reading: deadlocks are door locks that need a key, so the clue asks what opens many of them

explanation.walkthrough: A deadlock in the surface is a stalemate in talks; here it is a lock needing a key.
explanation.definitionFit: These are master keys with the wards filed down, so a single one can open many different locks.

clue.text: It's nothing to a rising lad giving the odd kiss to these lovelies

indicators.note: in a down entry, something rising goes upwards, so the word is read from bottom to top
odd means strange or irregular, telling us that word's letters come out in a peculiar order

blocks.note: O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young man playfully kisses a series of beautiful women, and it means nothing to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The odd kiss' looks like an occasional kiss, and 'odd' tempts you to take alternate letters; here it shuffles the whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: Odalisques were concubines or female slaves in a Turkish harem, often painted as beautiful reclining women.

clue.text: There's a sound resemblance here

blocks.note: surface reading: a solid, reliable likeness between two things
setter's reading: a likeness in sound, where vowel sounds echo each other

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like it means solid or valid, but it is about what you hear.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes words whose vowel sounds correspond, a partial rhyme heard in poetry.

clue.text: There's a lack of harmony here

definitions.text: There's a lack of harmony here

blocks.clueFragment: There's a lack of harmony here
blocks.note: surface reading: a place of discord or quarrelling
setter's reading: split into a negative prefix and a word for acting in harmony together

explanation.walkthrough: Concerted means acting together in harmony, and the prefix dis- undoes it, though the whole word means flustered.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means flustered or unsettled, and broken up it reads as 'not in concert', without harmony.

clue.text: Just a little letter from a Trollope notability, Sir

blocks.note: first meaning: the Greek letter whose name means 'little o'
second meaning: Sir ... Pie is the eminent physician in Trollope's Barchester novels

explanation.surface: A short note from a distinguished character in a Trollope novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little letter' sounds like a brief note; the Greek name literally means 'small o'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the fifteenth Greek letter, whose name means little o, and the first name of Trollope's doctor Sir Omicron Pie.

clue.text: The stuff of cordage is found in seaport

indicators.note: to found metal is to melt and recast it, so the following word is remade in a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Rope-making material turns up in a harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is found in' wants a hidden word, but the letters are not consecutive in any word; they are a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough Spanish and North African grass whose fibres are woven into rope, sandals and paper.

clue.text: Do this to d'oeil and get a blast!

definitions.text: Do this to d'oeil and get a blast!

blocks.note: setter's reading: the French phrase for a painting that deceives the eye, 'l'oeil' preceded by this word
setter's reading: also the name of a water-powered blowing device that supplies air to a forge

explanation.surface: A mock instruction to do something to an eye and get a blast of air.
explanation.walkthrough: The French verb means to deceive, as in the painting term; in English the word also names a device for blowing a furnace.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the first word of a French art term for illusionistic painting, and a forge blower driven by falling water.

clue.text: "Hunting he loved, but love he laugh'd to scorn"

definitions.text: "Hunting he loved, but love he laugh'd to scorn"

blocks.clueFragment: "Hunting he loved, but love he laugh'd to scorn"
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of verse about a huntsman who spurned love
setter's reading: a line from a Shakespeare narrative poem describing the beautiful youth whom the goddess of love courts

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a quotation; the solver must name the young hunter Shakespeare describes, who rejects Venus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's poem the goddess Venus woos the handsome youth, who prefers hunting and is killed by a boar.

clue.text: Where one was unlikely to get into hot water?

definitions.text: Where one was unlikely to get into hot water?

blocks.clueFragment: Where one was unlikely to get into hot water?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who is never in trouble
setter's reading: the word heard as 'lion iced', somewhere frozen where nothing hot is found

explanation.walkthrough: The word, meaning treated as a celebrity, is read as 'lion iced'; a celebrity so admired is unlikely to be in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: To be fêted as a celebrity is to be treated as a social lion, so one would hardly fall into disgrace.

clue.text: Give us a copper and be saved

blocks.note: a beggar's 'spare us a coin' asks you to give
D stood for a penny in British pre-decimal money, a copper coin

explanation.surface: A beggar's plea for a penny, promising salvation in return.
explanation.walkthrough: D, from the Latin denarius, was the old British penny; 'copper' is not a policeman here.
explanation.definitionFit: To be spared is to be let off or rescued from harm, so the past participle matches rescued.

clue.text: More? No, it's finished

blocks.note: first meaning: in excess of
second meaning: ended, done with

explanation.surface: Someone asks for another helping and is told it has all gone.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means in excess of a number, and also completed or at an end.

clue.text: I'm among top, performers, a flighty lot

indicators.note: 'I am among' puts a thing in the midst of others, surrounded by them, so this letter sits inside the following word

blocks.note: taken as written
stars are the top performers

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of mixing with top performers, a fickle crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty' suggests the performers are capricious; it means made up of flights, as a staircase is.
explanation.definitionFit: Steps arranged in flights are this, so a flighty collection is a punning description of a staircase.

clue.text: Jonson's humorous type, in a word

blocks.note: setter's reading: Ben Jonson wrote a comedy about men each ruled by their humour, an old word for temperament
setter's reading: the first two words of that play's title run together into one

explanation.surface: A comic character from Ben Jonson summed up briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: Humour here is the old medical sense of temperament, from Jonson's play title.
explanation.definitionFit: Running the play title's opening words together gives the term for an ordinary typical person, also the medieval morality play.

clue.text: Saints in shining array

definitions.note: adjective here, but the answer is a plural noun: glossy fabrics

indicators.note: to array is to set out in a new order, so the preceding word's letters are laid out afresh

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Holy figures dressed in gleaming robes.
explanation.definitionFit: These are glossy silk fabrics with a lustrous face, so shining clothing is made of them.

clue.text: Horses men and ships

blocks.note: first meaning: cavalry horses
second meaning: cavalry soldiers or mounted police
third meaning: troopships carrying soldiers

explanation.surface: A list of military assets: cavalry mounts, soldiers and vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers a cavalry soldier, a cavalry mount, and a vessel used for transporting soldiers.
